newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong issues code of banking practices.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong issues code of banking practices.

text.p: Hong Kong's key banking organisations on Friday released a non-statutory Code of Banking Practices meant to guide local banks' relationships with their clients.

The code was jointly issued by the Hong Kong Association of Banks (HKAB) and the Deposit-taking Companies Association (DTCA) following several months of public consultation on a draft version of the code released in January.
The Code has been developed by a working group comprising representatives of the industry associations and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).
"The Code will further enhance the transparency and quality of banking services in Hong Kong," said Raymond Li, executive director of banking policy at the HKMA.
"We fully endorse the provisions of the Code and we will monitor compliance as part of our regular supervision," he said.
The Code addresses relationships between banks and customers, the opening and operation of accounts and loans, card services, payment services and debt collection.
Banks are expected to observe the Code, but it is not legally binding.
Li said the HKMA would not take any action against those accused by customers of violating the Code.
He said "it would be up to the courts" to decide whether the Code could be enforced by law.
"The code does not dictate to banks how to run their operations in keeping with Hong Kong's principal of a free market within a regulatory framework," said HKAB Secretary Guy Priestly.
Most of the HKAB's 182 members already comply with the Code, he said.
Neither the HKMA, the HKAB nor the DTCA plan to set up special committees to monitor compliance with the Code.

The HKMA's Li said banks should achieve full compliance with the Code within six months of its July 14 effective date, but a further six months would be allowed for compliance with those parts that require system changes.
The Code as adopted is not very different from the draft version, but some alterations were made.
For example, wording governing the issuance of credit cards to students was made more general.
The first draft stipulated that banks notify the student's parents before issuing cards, but this suggestion was challenged on privacy grounds.
The new Code states only that banks "should act responsibly" when marketing cards to people "who may not have independent financial means", including students.
The HKMA and the banking groups are studying other ways to determine if a customer should be offered a credit card.
"It may be better to allow credit agencies to keep information on how many cards a person is holding and provide it to the banks," said Li.
This suggestion already has been submitted to Hong Kong's Privacy Commission for consideration, Li said.
Privacy rights enshrined in the Code generally exceed those stipulated by the Privacy Commission, he added.
